notes: \cpara{Announces that the post will name a current theory flawed in the same way as phlogiston and vitalism, the examples of ``Fake Causality'' and ``Mysterious Answers to Mysterious Questions.''}

\cpara{Names emergence and gives a definition. The quotation matches the first sentence of Wikipedia's article as it stood on 25 August 2007, the day before the post. The same article's next section, ``Definitions,'' gives narrower senses: the coinage of G.~H. Lewes (1875), who set ``emergents'' against ``resultants,'' which are ``a sum or a difference of the co-operant forces,'' and a distinction between ``weak'' and ``strong'' emergence.}
\cpara{Argues that the definition fits everything above quarks, so that ``It's an emergent phenomenon!'' explains no more than ``It's not a quark!''}

\clogic{True of the one-line summary the post quotes, not of the narrower definitions. For C.~D. Broad (1925), a property of a whole is emergent only if it ``cannot, even in theory, be deduced from the most complete knowledge of the properties'' of its parts. In that sense, calling something emergent is a claim that can turn out false. The \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Emergent Properties'') reports that the view waned as later science, above all quantum chemistry and molecular biochemistry, eroded the boundaries between levels.}

\cpara{Narrows the target to the noun used as an explanation; the verb ``emerges from'' is acceptable before a specific model. The narrowing is fair. The first paragraph, which named emergence as a flawed ``theory,'' is not narrowed to match.}
\cpara{A joke: ``arisence'' offered as the explanation of gravity.}
\cpara{Restates when ``emerges from'' is acceptable: before a specific model.}
\cpara{Claims that ``emergence'' is commonly used as an explanation in its own right. The evidence is in the next paragraph.}

\cpara{The evidence is what the author has ``heard people say,'' with no speaker named and no text quoted. Such writers have existed: Samuel Alexander wrote in 1920 that life, an emergent quality, must ``be accepted with the `natural piety' of the investigator. It admits no explanation'' (quoted in the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}). But the post's targets are present-day speakers about intelligence, and none is quoted. The same pattern recurs three days later in ``Say Not `Complexity'{}.''}
\cpara{Applies the fourth sign of a mysterious answer: after ``Emergence'' the phenomenon is still a mystery.}
\cpara{Proposes deleting ``emergent'' from a sentence to see whether its meaning changes.}

\clogic{This ``Even better'' sentence is close to what some defenders of the term mean by it. In the words of the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, Mark Bedau (1997) counts a feature as weakly emergent when it is ``derivable from the prior micro-facts leading up to it, but only in an informationally incompressible way,'' that is, by running the parts forward, as a model of individual ants does. The Wikipedia article the post links describes its ant colony the same way: ``each ant is an autonomous unit that reacts depending only on its local environment.''}
\cpara{Proposes replacing ``emergent'' with ``magical,'' the word used ``before emergence was invented.''}

\clogic{In C.~D. Broad's usage (1925), ``Life is an emergent phenomenon'' says something that ``Life is a magical phenomenon'' does not: that life needs no special substance. Broad set ``Emergent Vitalism'' against ``Substantial Vitalism,'' which posits ``a peculiar component, often called an `Entelechy','' and rejected the entelechy for reasons much like the post's against ``Élan vital.'' The substitution erases what the word ruled out, a life-substance, which is the error the previous post charged vitalism with.}
\cpara{Asks whether each pair of sentences does not fit ``exactly the same set of outcomes.''}

\clogic{The Wikipedia article the post links had already made the comparison, for one sense of the word. It quotes Bedau (1997): ``Although strong emergence is logically possible, it is uncomfortably like magic.'' Bedau defended weak emergence. The post applies to the word in general a comparison that its own source made for one sense.}

\cpara{Explains the word's popularity: it is ``the junk food of curiosity'' and ``gives you a sacred mystery to worship.'' No evidence is given for this cause. The \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} gives another: attention to emergence ``was substantially reinvigorated starting in the 1970s with the discovery and creation of non-linear complex systems.''}
\cpara{Ends on the people who use the word, not on the word. The phrase ``literary genre'' repeats ``Science as Attire'' (23 August 2007).}
